headline: Bunker Pods Off Holgate Turned the Beachfront Into a Feeding Line
subhead: The blitz we said was coming from Belmar finally showed up at the jetties, but stripers went nocturnal while bluefish took over the daylight.
body_markdown:
Ran the drone over the Holgate stretch Tuesday morning and the water told me everything before I even rigged a rod. Big dark ovals — bunker, thousands of them — pushed tight against the beach from the old Coast Guard station down toward the tip, and under them, that nervous, flashing chop that means blues are already in the school. By the time I got down there with a rod, the birds had found it too. Terns diving, a few gulls working the edges, and every third or fourth minute the whole pod would explode white for a second and go quiet again.

We flagged this last week — said the bunker pods pushing south from the Belmar blitz zone would funnel past Barnegat and Beach Haven on the tide changes, and that's exactly what's playing out. The bait's been thick enough that you don't need to guess where the fish are, you just need to get there before the pod moves. That's been the trick all week — this isn't a park-and-wait bite, it's a drive-the-beach-and-watch bite.

The blues have been the most honest fish out there right now. Cocktails to mid-teens crashing bunker from Barnegat Light down through Ship Bottom, and when a pod pins up against the jetty rocks at the inlet on the last of the incoming, it gets stupid for ten or fifteen minutes. Bucktails with a strip of bunker belly draped off the hook have worked, but honestly a naked white Ava 27 ripped through the school on a fast retrieve is just as deadly and you don't lose a lure to a cutoff every other cast. Guys throwing poppers into the boils off the north end of Holgate have had some of the most violent surface strikes I've seen all summer — topwater explosions that'll put a hitch in your heart rate.

Stripers are a different animal right now, and this is where I have to be straight with you — the daytime bass bite has gone quiet. Water's pushing into the mid-70s along the beachfront and that's shoved the bass off the surface layer entirely. They're down deep during daylight, probably holding on the thermocline break off the outer bars, and they've gone almost fully nocturnal. If you want stripers this week, you're fishing dawn, dusk, or full dark — no way around it. I worked the trough off Brant Beach at first light Wednesday with a black/purple Danny plug, slow swim through the inside slough, and picked up two schoolies in the 24-26 inch range before the sun got high enough to shut it down. Nothing to write home about, but it confirms they're still there, just working a tighter window.

Little Egg Inlet and the cut at Holgate are worth your time on the night tide — that structure holds current even when the moon's not doing much for you, and bass will slide up onto the edge of the bar to ambush bait moving through on the ebb. Bucktails in the 1 to 1.5 ounce range, white or chartreuse, bounced along the bottom of the cut on the outgoing has been the most consistent producer after dark. Don't overwork it — let the current do the work and just keep contact.

Fluke has cooled off exactly like it does every year once the shallow water heats up like this. The inshore humps in Barnegat Bay that were holding fish in June have gone quiet during the day, but the channel edges near the causeway bridge and the deeper humps off Ship Bottom are still giving up keepers on the stronger stages of the tide — moving water is doing all the work for you right now. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the channel drop where it meets the flat, has been the pattern. Morning incoming has outproduced the afternoon for us — cooler water, more willing fish. Shorts are everywhere if you want numbers, but you've got to work the deeper edges for anything over 18 inches.

Weakfish have been a rumor more than a pattern up here — nothing consistent to report on the LBI side, though I'd keep an ear out if that Delaware Bay resurgence starts pushing fish up the coast. Kingfish have shown in small numbers on bloodworm rigs off the surf at Beach Haven on the calmer mornings, nothing to build a trip around but a nice bonus if you're already out there for blues.

Tide-wise, work the last two hours of the incoming at the inlets for the bluefish blitz — that's when bait gets pushed tight against structure and the blues pin them. For bass, you want the first hour of the outgoing after dark at Little Egg and Holgate, when moving water pulls bait off the flats into the cut. Wind's been light out of the southwest most mornings, which is keeping the surf manageable, but it's building a little haze and warming the shallows even more — expect the bass pattern to stay nocturnal as long as this holds.

Looking ahead, if the bunker keep working north past Holgate like they have been, this blitz should stay hot through the weekend — I'd bet on it holding at least another 72 hours unless a wind shift scatters the bait. Best case, the pods stack up right on the Beach Haven side and give the pier and jetty guys a shot without even needing a boat. Worst case, a stiff onshore blow pushes everything out past the bar and we're back to searching. Either way, I'd rather be on the beach at first light with a topwater in hand than sitting home wondering.
